analysis.one_liner: Loosens federal banking rules: cuts consumer disclosures, caps bank liability, and weakens community reinvestment oversight.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 63 bipartisan cosponsors, cleared a House Banking subcommittee on a 13-6 vote in June 1995 but never got a full committee or floor vote; its provisions were sent on to a different bill.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have cut the paperwork and rules that banks, thrifts, and credit unions must follow. It would have trimmed or repealed consumer protections on everything from savings-account disclosures to mortgage rescission rights, expanded what customers must pay when cards or accounts are used without permission, let small banks certify their own compliance with the Community Reinvestment Act, and let well-capitalized banking companies buy other banks with less regulatory review. Supporters argued the rules were outdated paperwork that raised costs for banks and their customers.
analysis.who_benefits: Depository institutions (banks, thrifts, credit unions) and bank holding companies gain most: they would face fewer disclosure mandates, lower compliance and liability exposure, self-certification under the Community Reinvestment Act, streamlined merger and acquisition approvals, and fewer reporting requirements for insider loans. Loan buyers and servicers gain narrower liability when mortgage disclosures were wrong. Some provisions help consumers directly: clearer leasing-cost tables, simpler credit-denial notices, and a ban on misleading deposit advertisements.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Banks, thrifts, and bank holding companies

how_it_helps.text: Repeals most Truth in Savings Act disclosure requirements (interest-rate and fee schedules, periodic statements) while keeping a ban on misleading advertisements, leaving customers with less standardized information to compare accounts [S2][S3].

Caps and in places retroactively wipes out bank liability for mortgage disclosure errors, limits homeowners' right to rescind certain refinancings, and requires consumers to show they relied on a wrong disclosure before recovering actual damages [S2][S3].

Expands customer liability for unauthorized electronic transfers and credit-card use — including up to $500 when a customer writes a PIN on a card and liability for transactions by someone the customer authorized — and lets a bank's affiliates freely share customer information with a one-time opt-out [S2][S3].

Exempts small banks from Community Reinvestment Act examinations, lets banks under $250 million self-certify compliance, and bars regulators from imposing new CRA recordkeeping; it also raises the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act reporting threshold from $10 million to $50 million in assets [S2][S3].

Lets well-capitalized, well-managed banking organizations acquire banks and nonbank companies with notice instead of prior approval, and eliminates merger filings, branch and ATM applications, and many other filings [S2][S3].

Includes genuine consumer gains: itemized tabular leasing disclosures, combined and simplified adverse-action notices, safe-harbor protection only for statistically sound credit-scoring systems, and elimination of recordkeeping for executive-officer loans while allowing broad employee benefit-plan loans [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Bank customers and communities. Consumers would have less information to compare savings accounts, fewer ways to undo improper mortgage refinancings, more responsibility for fraudulent card and account use, and weaker control over how their financial data is shared. Neighborhoods would have less leverage over banks' community lending records, since regulators could no longer require CRA loan data and thousands of banks would report no mortgage-lending data at all.

drawbacks.text: The consumer-protection rollbacks are the strongest objection: repealing Truth in Savings disclosures, narrowing rescission rights and damages, expanding liability for unauthorized transfers, and allowing affiliate information sharing all shift risk and information costs onto customers [S2][S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge the burden argument cuts both ways: some rules do impose real compliance costs on small banks that can translate into fees or fewer services, but many targeted rules — CRA data, HMDA reporting, insider-loan records — are exactly what lets regulators and the public see what banks are doing with deposits and lending [S2][S3].

Critics of self-certification and self-testing privileges would note they let banks police their own compliance with fair-lending and community reinvestment law, with results shielded from use by applicants in lawsuits [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Some streamlining — merging duplicative merger approvals, clearing up conflicting disclosure rules between Truth in Lending and RESPA, simplifying credit-denial notices — is defensible on its own terms. But the bill's core trades away disclosure, liability, and community-lending oversight in exchange for lower bank compliance costs, and the consumer-facing provisions it does add (leasing disclosure tables, simpler notices) are small next to the protections it removes. On balance it is structured for the benefit of regulated institutions.

outcome.mechanism: After the House Banking subcommittee approved an amended version 13-6, the bill never came before the full committee or the House floor; on June 28, 1995 the record points further action to a separate bill, H.R. 1858, and the 104th Congress ended without this one becoming law.

narrative.text: Introduced March 30, 1995 by Rep. Doug Bereuter with 63 cosponsors (53 Republicans, 10 Democrats) and referred to the House Banking and Financial Services Committee [S1][S4][S5].

The Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit subcommittee held four hearings in May and June 1995, then marked the bill up and forwarded it to the full committee in amended form by a 13-6 vote [S5].

On June 28, 1995 the record states 'For Further Action See H.R.1858,' indicating the bill's provisions were routed into the committee's broader regulatory-relief vehicle rather than advancing on their own; no full committee markup, floor vote, or Senate action on H.R. 1362 appears in the record, and the Congress ended January 3, 1997 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Bank customers and communities that depend on Community Reinvestment Act and disclosure rules are better off, because the protections this bill would have trimmed — savings-account disclosure, rescission rights, limits on liability for fraud, and CRA data — remained in place. Banks did not obtain the compliance relief in this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Bank customers and community lending advocates

industries.industry: Banks, thrifts, and bank holding companies
industries.note: The bill cuts their compliance costs across deposit, mortgage, and lending rules and eases merger and branch approvals, but the savings come from rules that protect customers and give communities visibility into bank lending. CRA self-certification and the ban on new CRA data collection would also lock in weaker public oversight of community lending.
Narrower assignee liability, tighter rescission deadlines, retroactive liability waivers, and a harder damages test reduce the cost of disclosure mistakes, shifting that risk to borrowers [S3].
The bill reduces assessments on appraisers but abolishes the federal Appraisal Subcommittee and folds its functions into the examination council, loosening oversight of appraisal standards [S2].
